title: Raft
description: Master Raft consensus: leader election with randomized timeouts, log replication, commit index advancement, safety guarantees, and etcd's production implementation.

segments.text: Diego Ongaro designed Raft in 2014 with one explicit goal: be understandable. Where Paxos is mathematically elegant but operationally opaque, Raft is mechanically clear. It decomposes consensus into three sub-problems: leader election, log replication, and safety. Let's build it up piece by piece.

Every Raft node is in one of three states: Follower, Candidate, or Leader. All nodes start as Followers. If a Follower doesn't hear from the Leader within its election timeout, it becomes a Candidate and starts an election. Time is divided into terms, each with at most one leader. Terms are logical clocks that increase monotonically.

Leader election uses randomized timeouts to avoid split votes. Each Follower picks a random election timeout between 150 and 300 milliseconds. The first to timeout becomes a Candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote to all peers. If it gets votes from a majority, it's the new Leader. The randomization makes simultaneous candidates rare.

Split votes can still happen. Two nodes timeout simultaneously, both become Candidates, and neither gets a majority. The solution: everyone resets with new random timeouts and tries again. In practice, split votes are resolved within one or two rounds. With a 150 millisecond randomization window, the odds of repeated splits are vanishingly small.
segments.thought_prompt: Why does randomization work better than a fixed timeout for preventing split votes?

segments.text: Once elected, the Leader handles all client writes. It appends the command to its log and sends AppendEntries RPCs to all Followers. Each Follower appends the entry to its own log and acknowledges. When the Leader receives acknowledgment from a majority, it commits the entry and applies it to the state machine. Committed entries are durable.

The commit index is how Followers know which entries are safe to apply. The Leader piggybacks its commit index on every AppendEntries message. When a Follower sees a commit index higher than its own, it applies all entries up to that index. This means Followers can lag behind but will always catch up. No entry is applied until the Leader confirms majority replication.

Raft's safety guarantee: a Candidate can only win an election if its log is at least as up-to-date as a majority. When processing RequestVote, a node rejects the vote if the Candidate's last log entry has a lower term, or the same term but fewer entries. This ensures the new Leader has all committed entries, no rollback needed.

Compared to Paxos: Raft uses a strong leader, so there's no dueling proposers problem. Log entries are always contiguous, no gaps. The protocol is specified completely, including leader election and membership changes. The trade-off: Raft's strong leader means all writes go through one node, which can be a throughput bottleneck.
segments.thought_prompt: If the strong leader is a throughput bottleneck, what are the options for scaling writes?

segments.text: etcd is Raft's most important production implementation. It's the brain of every Kubernetes cluster, storing all cluster state. etcd's Raft implementation handles snapshots for log compaction, learner nodes for safe cluster expansion, and linearizable reads through the leader. When your kubectl command works, thank etcd's Raft implementation.

Raft succeeded where Paxos struggled: in making consensus implementable. The proof is in the ecosystem. etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV, Consul, all use Raft. When you need a replicated log with strong consistency, Raft is almost certainly your starting point. Understand the three sub-problems, and you understand distributed consensus.
